title: Behavioral Science for Researchers
description: Strengthen research practice, collaboration, and responsible evidence use.

questions.prompt: When a protocol changes after data collection begins, a researcher should:
options: Document and justify the change, following oversight requirements
Hide it to preserve the original plan
Rewrite the date of the protocol
questions.explanation: Transparent records and required ethics review let others assess deviations and participant protections.

questions.prompt: Preregistration prevents researchers from conducting exploratory analyses.
questions.explanation: Exploration remains useful; it should be distinguished from analyses specified in advance.

questions.prompt: Which support responsible data stewardship?
questions.explanation: A data-management plan anticipates security, documentation, access, and retention needs.

questions.prompt: Authorship should reflect meaningful scholarly contribution and responsibility for the work.
questions.explanation: Contributor roles and accountability should be discussed transparently, using relevant field standards.

questions.prompt: A reviewer who has a serious conflict of interest should:
options: Disclose it to the editor and follow their guidance
Use the review to advance a competing project
questions.explanation: Editors need disclosure to decide whether impartial review is possible.

questions.prompt: Peer review guarantees that a published study is correct.
questions.explanation: Peer review can improve work but cannot eliminate error, bias, or uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which help prevent p-hacking?
options: Try many specifications and report only one
questions.explanation: Transparency makes analytic flexibility visible; exploratory work can still generate hypotheses.

questions.prompt: A null result can be scientifically useful when reported with methods and uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Well-described null estimates can update evidence and inform future study design.

questions.prompt: When communicating a limitation, a researcher should:
questions.explanation: Specific limitations help readers judge how far findings can reasonably be generalized.

questions.prompt: A convenience sample can support every population-level claim if the sample is large.
questions.explanation: Size does not remove selection bias; population inference needs a defensible sampling or transport argument.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for collaborative projects?
options: Assume all collaborators share the same priorities
questions.explanation: Explicit roles, records, and authorship conversations reduce preventable conflict.

questions.prompt: A researcher should correct the record when a material error is discovered in published work.
questions.explanation: Timely correction helps preserve the integrity of the scholarly record.

questions.prompt: An effect size is most useful when interpreted with:
questions.explanation: Magnitude only becomes meaningful relative to scale, precision, and substantive context.

questions.prompt: Sharing data is always required even when consent or privacy protections prohibit it.
questions.explanation: Ethical and legal commitments can limit open sharing; controlled access or synthetic data may help.

questions.prompt: Which habits make a research analysis easier to reproduce?
questions.explanation: Code, computational environment, and data definitions help others reconstruct analysis.

questions.prompt: A statistically significant finding should be interpreted in light of multiplicity and prior evidence.
questions.explanation: Selective testing and publication can distort apparent certainty; cumulative evidence matters.

questions.prompt: When a collaborator raises a concern about research integrity, the best response is to:
options: Preserve relevant records and use appropriate reporting channels
questions.explanation: Preserving evidence and following institutional procedures supports fair, confidential inquiry.

questions.prompt: Which support inclusive research participation?
options: Compensation that is fair and non-coercive
Excluding groups without a scientific rationale
questions.explanation: Accessible communication and fair recruitment improve respect and relevance while preserving voluntary consent.

questions.prompt: A limitation should be interpreted as a boundary on claims, not a reason to dismiss all findings.
questions.explanation: Limitations constrain inference; their importance depends on the claim and design.

questions.prompt: A citation should support the specific claim for which it is provided.
questions.explanation: Accurate, relevant sourcing lets readers trace evidence and assess whether it warrants the statement.
